You are part of an optimization system that improves a given text (i.e. the variable). You are the gradient (feedback) engine. Your only responsibility is to give intelligent and creative feedback and constructive criticism to variables, given an objective specified in <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> </OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> tags. The variables may be solutions to problems, prompts to language models, code, or any other text-based variable. Pay attention to the role description of the variable, and the context in which it is used. You should assume that the variable will be used in a similar context in the future. Only provide strategies, explanations, and methods to change in the variable. DO NOT propose a new version of the variable, that will be the job of the optimizer. Your only job is to send feedback and criticism (compute 'gradients'). For instance, feedback can be in the form of 'Since language models have the X failure mode...', 'Adding X can fix this error because...', 'Removing X can improve the objective function because...', 'Changing X to Y would fix the mistake ...', that gets at the downstream objective.
If a variable is already working well (e.g. the objective function is perfect, an evaluation shows the response is accurate), you should not give feedback.

### Glossary of tags that will be sent to you:

# - <LM_INPUT>: The input to the language model.
# - <LM_OUTPUT>: The output of the language model.
# - <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION>: The objective of the optimization task.
# - <VARIABLE>: Specifies the span of the variable.
# - <ROLE>: The role description of the variable.
payload.instruction: Make her close her jacket fully
payload.rubric: Judge requested image editing: yes means all requested changes are complete, no means no requested change has progressed, partial means some progress without complete fulfillment. Unrelated edits are not requested progress. Insufficient evidence stays unresolved.

node.question: Compared with the source image, has the jacket's front closure visibly moved toward closing in the edited image, such as the front panels coming closer together along the closure?
node.criteria: Pass if the edited image visibly shows the front panels closer together along the closure than in the source, even if an opening remains; fail if the closure is visibly no closer together or more open than in the source; unknown if the closure or its source-to-edited change cannot be judged.
node.binding: Assess progress only on the requested jacket closure, comparing the same closure in the source and edited images; this is not a substitute for the fully closed endpoint.
node.endpoint: The jacket's front panels have visibly moved closer together along the closure compared with the source.
node.necessity: The rubric distinguishes no requested change from partial progress. A separate comparison is needed because the existing full-closure check fails both when there is no progress and when there is incomplete progress. The images show an open jacket in both, but the changed pose and drape do not by themselves establish closure progress.

node_traces.evidence: The jacket remains visibly open in both images. In the edited image, the front panels do not appear closer together along the closure; the jacket instead hangs open and flares outward on her right side.

d1_complete: The trace is valid and clearly observes a broad opening in the edited jacket, so this is not a transport, schema, or dependency failure. The node’s strict endpoint criterion is also faithful to “fully”; do not weaken it or treat partial progress as completion. However, the reference says yes while the visible edited image appears to show the jacket still open, and the trace reports high confidence. Investigate the reference/label alignment and whether the visual check is binding to the correct garment and closure in this changed pose; compare the edited image directly with the source, using visible closure evidence rather than the source state as a substitute. Keep uncertainty available if the closure is obscured, and avoid changing the criterion merely to force agreement with the aggregate label.

response.content: {"text":"The node is correctly scoped to closure progress rather than the fully closed endpoint, and its trace is valid; this is not a transport, schema, or dependency failure. But the comparison may be over-weighting the edited jacket’s visible open drape: the edited image shows the woman turned sideways, so the front closure is less directly visible than in the source. Refine the binding to track the same front closure across the pose change and assess any visible movement toward closure, distinguishing an obscured/uncertain closure from clear evidence of no progress. Do not infer progress from the changed pose or jacket flare, and do not relax the criterion to force agreement with the reference label. The high-confidence disagreement also warrants checking reference/label alignment; the aggregate label is not atomic ground truth."}
